# SMELT: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers

English · [简体中文](../zh/2609.01343.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2609.01343 · 2026-09-01 · Tsinghua University, ByteDance Seed, M-A-P, TokenWave.AI</sub>

<img src="../../assets/glyphs/2609.01343.svg" alt="L1-3 (3 layers) -&gt; [L4-9 (6 layers)] x 2 -&gt; L10-12 (3 layers); injection none; KV per-pass">

> With per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache matched, looping the middle half of an MoE Transformer twice lowers loss at four scales up to 54B non-embedding parameters and saves 6.8-18.0% of training FLOPs on the fitted frontier.

**Category**: Scaling and budget · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 38 · HF upvotes 86

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01343)

## Problem

Most looped-model gains are reported at fixed parameter count, where the looped model also spends more FLOPs and KV cache, so architecture and extra compute are conflated; the paper asks whether looping still helps when per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache are all held fixed.

## Method

- Pay for the extra pass by narrowing the hidden size (1280 to 1056 at 200M, S ≈ 95%), recover total parameters by adding experts (192 to 288 per layer), and use smaller heads at a higher GQA ratio to keep the KV cache within 4%.
- Choose the recipe with three 200M ablations under these budgets; loop the middle 50% of layers twice, keep the Baseline's physical depth, and scale each looped sublayer's residual update by 1/r.
- Train matched Baseline / SMELT pairs over 4 scales x 4 sparsity levels with six WSD decay branches each (up to about 215B tokens), and fit a separate Chinchilla-style law L(F, S, D) per architecture to compare compute-optimal frontiers.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | MoE |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (L4-9) | train 2; test 2 |
| Backprop (L4-9) | both passes |

Shown for the 200M scale (L = 12) used in all design ablations; the middle 6 of 12 layers run twice, so 18 layers execute per token. All four scales loop the middle 50% twice and place ⌊(L − m)/2⌋ layers before the span (looped layers 3-7, 4-9, 6-15 and 8-22 for L = 10, 12, 20 and 30). Inside the loop each sublayer's residual update is scaled by 1/r (here 1/2), and every layer execution computes its own Q, K and V; smaller heads at a higher GQA ratio keep the KV cache close to the Baseline's.

## Other findings

- At 200M with all budgets matched, looping the middle 6 of 12 layers gives lower validation loss than looping all 12 (1.9257 vs 1.9322 at S ≈ 85%, 1.8517 vs 1.8601 at S ≈ 95%), and every span tested beats the unlooped Baseline. (Section 3.3; Table 3)
- Two passes beat three and four at matched FLOPs, parameters and KV (validation loss 1.9257 vs 1.9385 and 1.9360, DCLM Core 27.57 vs 27.15 and 27.30); the authors attribute the regression to the narrower model that extra passes force. (Section 3.5; Table 5)
- SMELT's fitted capacity and data exponents are both larger (a = 0.3892 vs 0.3703, c = 0.7011 vs 0.6594), giving frontier exponents of 0.250 vs 0.237; the irreducible losses differ by 0.005 nats, less than either fit's RMSE. (Section 4.3; Table 6)
- SMELT wins 96 of 96 matched pairs on DCLM Completion, 83 of 96 on DCLM Core and 29 of the 30 MMLU pairs whose Baseline is at least 10 points above chance, and it scores better than a Baseline at the same validation loss would (positive mean residual on all three at every scale). (Section 5.1; Figures 5-9)
- The gain is larger on longer samples and with in-context examples; the loss improvement on the four longest length buckets is 1.52x that on the four shortest, and the few-shot accuracy gap widens from 0.9 pp at k = 0 to 1.9 pp at k = 1, holding through k = 8. (Section 5.3; Figure 11)
- The second visit shrinks the attention sink; for the 1.6B Dyck head, BOS attention mass falls from 0.60 to 0.02 and mass on demonstration answers rises from 0.24 to 0.85. (Section 6.4; Figure 18)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Unlooped MoE Transformer from the same internal family (top-8 routing, GQA), trained on identical token sequences in each of 16 grid cells (four scales; S = 0% and S ≈ 85%, 95%, 97%).
- **Held fixed**: F (training FLOPs), N (unique parameters), KV (KV cache per token), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: A (active parameters), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: With per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters and KV cache matched (typical mismatch under 4%, 1% and 4%), SMELT reaches lower loss than the Baseline at every scale and sparsity level, and its separately fitted frontier saves 6.8-18.0% of training FLOPs at 10^20-10^21 FLOPs (14.7% at 10^21 and S ≈ 97%). (Abstract; Section 1; Table 2; Table 7)

## Caveats

- Active parameters and executed depth are not matched; at 200M and S ≈ 95% SMELT has 0.142B active parameters against the Baseline's 0.209B and executes 18 layers instead of 12 (Section 3.2; Tables 9-10).
- The span, depth and loop-count ablations ran only at 200M, with one training run per configuration and the same loop count in training and evaluation; the authors note the best span or count may differ at larger scales (Section 3.3; Section 7).
- Budget matching equates arithmetic FLOPs, parameters and KV-cache size, not wall-clock cost (Section 7).
- The model family and training stack are proprietary and cannot be released, pretraining uses an internal corpus, and training contexts are 4096 tokens (Section 3.1; Appendix A).
- SMELT shares the Baseline's optimizer, schedule and data; the Baseline configurations come from a tuned MoE family, and no separate tuning for SMELT is reported (Section 3.1; Appendix A).
